knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 2.6.2
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly distinguishes a statistic, its sampling distribution, and one realised value from one sample?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: The learning objective separates the statistic, its repeated-sample distribution, and one realised draw.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Statistic = function of sample; sampling distribution = law over repeated samples; realised value = one draw.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Collapsing the realised value into the sampling distribution.

choices.label: A statistic is a function of the sample. Its sampling distribution is the distribution of that statistic over repeated random samples. One realised value is a single draw from that distribution, not the distribution itself.
A statistic is a fixed population parameter, and its sampling distribution is that same constant number.
The sampling distribution is the single realised sample mean from the data set you hold, and repeated-sample language is optional.
A realised statistic equals its sampling distribution whenever the sample size is larger than 30.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 2.6.2
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. A colleague says my sample mean is 12, so the sampling distribution is 12. Which statement is correct?
knowledge_checks.body: Refuse the collapse; restate the LO.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: A realised statistic is one draw; the sampling distribution is the repeated-sample law.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Refuse equating the realised mean with the sampling distribution; describe the repeated-sample distribution of the statistic.

choices.label: Refuse: a realised statistic is not its sampling distribution. The skill is describing the distribution of the statistic over repeated samples.
Accept: the sampling distribution equals whatever number the current sample mean takes.
Refuse only if n is small; for large n the realised mean is the sampling distribution.
The claim is correct because parameters and sampling distributions are the same object once a mean is computed.
